title: Cruise Ships and Container Huts: Asian Games 2026 Faces Bed Crunch Before Liftoff
excerpt: With 17,000 athletes and officials descending on Nagoya and Aichi — more than the Olympics — organizers have scrapped the athletes' village for a cruise liner, hotels and wooden containers, and not everyone is sleeping easy.
body:
• The 20th Asian Games open Saturday, September 19 in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture and run to October 4, with athletes from 45 countries and territories across more than 40 sports.
  • More than 17,000 competitors and officials have registered — exceeding the 15,000 organizers planned for — forcing a scramble for beds in hotels, wooden container units and the cruise ship Costa Serena.
  • South Korean officials branded the facilities "the worst" accommodation ever at the Games, citing beds too short and "a serious shortage of accommodation," while record rain forced brief evacuations last week.
  • India built replica container units at SAI centers in Patiala and Bengaluru so its athletes — expected to number 700-plus, its biggest-ever contingent — can acclimatize before flying to Japan.

Seventeen thousand guests, not enough beds

The Asian Games open in Japan on Saturday with 2028 Olympic places up for grabs, some of world sport's fastest-rising talents in action — and thousands of athletes sleeping on a cruise ship during typhoon season. More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected at the continent's biggest sporting event, which runs September 19 to October 4 across Nagoya and the wider Aichi prefecture. That number — larger than the Olympics — has become a sore point for stretched organizers, who planned for 15,000 and have been scrambling to find beds for the rest.

https://x.com/WENewsEnglish/status/2099876004218990778

Organizers chose temporary accommodation to cut costs — a cruise liner, wooden container units and hotel rooms — and insist the 20th edition will be "the most spectacular for generations," with a bed for everyone.

The floating village

Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes and officials will stay on the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena — 571 cabins, seven pools, eight restaurants, nine bars. Cruise ships have housed athletes before, but never on this scale. Another 2,400 will stay in modular wooden units at Garden Pier; the rest are spread across hotels mapped to venues.

On Monday, South Korean officials branded the facilities "the worst" accommodation ever at the Games, citing beds too short and "a serious shortage of accommodation," a Korean Olympic committee official told AFP. Record rainfall forced athletes to briefly evacuate last week, rainwater seeped into some venues, and more rain is forecast — in the middle of typhoon season.

India builds its own rehearsal

India is not leaving the adjustment to chance. The Sports Authority of India built replica container units at its Patiala and Bengaluru centers — 40-foot boxes with two twin bedrooms, two bathrooms, a small kitchen and a living area — and rostered athletes to spend nights in them before flying to Japan.

"These containers are like a simulator," Vineet Kumar, deputy director general of the SAI, told AFP in Patiala. "It is a unique concept as never in an Asian Games or Olympics this kind of accommodation was used. So specifically we created this to make sure that our athletes don't feel the shock and get claustrophobic when they are given such accommodation in Japan."

"A player's psychology is so strong that if there is any problem in such logistics then their level of competition gets affected and we took care of this."

— Vineet Kumar, deputy director general, Sports Authority of India

India has asked organizers to place its athletes in on-land accommodation rather than the ship, sparing shooters and weightlifters pre-competition discomfort. The contingent should exceed 700 athletes across 35 disciplines — India's biggest-ever Asian Games team, with athletics contributing 73. Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya has promised full support on training, sports science, logistics, food and medical care: "our athletes are our top priority."

The sporting stakes

The sport itself is stacked. Athletes from 45 countries and territories will compete in more than 40 sports, with the Games doubling as LA 2028 qualifiers in seven sports including surfing, tennis, archery and squash. Start lists glitter: Philippine tennis star Alexandra Eala, 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Taiwan's Lin Yu-ting boxes two years after her Paris gold amid the gender-eligibility row; hosts Japan lean on gymnast Shinnosuke Oka and javelin thrower Haruka Kitaguchi. North Korea brings 100-plus athletes; China sends 800-plus, including 36 Olympic champions, after 201 golds at Hangzhou 2023.

Cricket returns with an edge: Sooryavanshi's India could meet Pakistan in the final at Nagoya's new purpose-built ground, ahead of the sport's Olympic return in Los Angeles after a 128-year absence. Some teams are unimpressed with venues — reports cite tents as dressing rooms and distant washrooms. Basketball and football are already underway; eSports, breakdancing and BMX target younger viewers, while padel and MMA debut.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the Games offer a rare double bill: a record-sized Indian contingent and the tantalizing prospect of an India-Pakistan cricket final on a global stage. Sooryavanshi, at 15, is the name diaspora households will be watching — the youngest member of the contingent carrying the oldest storyline in Asian sport.

What to watch

The opening ceremony is Saturday, with athletics and swimming to follow. The real test for organizers is logistical: keep 17,000 people fed, housed and dry through typhoon season. India's replica containers, meanwhile, get a second life after the Games — SAI plans to reuse them as guest rooms in Patiala and Bengaluru.
